recordings.title: Chat: Qwen3-30B-A3B across three DGX Sparks and a desktop CPU
recordings.summary: A scripted three-turn chat at temperature 0 with Qwen3-30B-A3B (48 layers, 128 experts, top 8, thinking on) over four processes (TASK-33): the three Sparks over RDMA, plus a desktop's CPU in WSL2 over TCP on the campus network, one router mixing both kinds of link. The desktop answers each expert call in about 1.4 ms against 0.06 ms on a Spark's GPU, so it sets the pace at 2.0 tokens/s; it plays at 4x by default. Its replies differ from the three-Spark chat because FP8 activations round differently when experts move.
recordings.note: A note on this reply: experts are not separate models trained on different tasks or topics. Each layer has its own experts, and its router picks a few of them for every token; those are the experts you see light up in the diagram.

recordings.title: Chat: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on one DGX Spark, experts streamed from NVMe
recordings.summary: A scripted three-turn chat at temperature 0 through the engine's OpenAI-compatible server (TASK-30), with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (TASK-31): 48 layers mixing Gated DeltaNet and attention, 512 experts chosen 10 at a time. The Q8_0 weights are larger than gx10-02's memory, so the experts stream from NVMe through a 12,000-slot cache on the GPU. It was recorded at 7 to 8 tokens/s with reasoning on.

recordings.title: Chat: OLMoE-1B-7B split across two DGX Sparks over RDMA
recordings.summary: A scripted three-turn chat at temperature 0 through the engine's OpenAI-compatible server (TASK-30), recorded with --record. Rank 0 on gx10-02 runs attention, the router and experts 0 to 31 of each layer; rank 1 on gx10-03 runs experts 32 to 63, reached over RDMA. The per-rank call counts below come from the frames and are checked against the engine's own counters.
recordings.note: A note on this reply: experts are not separate models trained on different tasks or topics. Each layer has its own experts, and its router picks a few of them for every token; those are the experts you see light up in the diagram.

recordings.title: Chat: Qwen3-30B-A3B through an expert cache, with prefetching
recordings.summary: The same scripted three-turn chat with Qwen3-30B-A3B on gx10-02, its 6,144 experts streamed from NVMe through a 3,000-slot cache, with the lookahead router guessing each next layer's experts (TASK-41). Each expert dot shows whether its call found the expert in memory, prefetched in time, still loading or missed, and the drive shows each load. Over the chat, 95.0% of calls found their expert in memory, 1.2% prefetched in time, 1.9% prefetched but late and 2.0% missed, against 4.2% missed without lookahead.
recordings.note: A note on this reply: experts are not separate models trained on different tasks or topics. Each layer has its own experts, and its router picks a few of them for every token; those are the experts you see light up in the diagram.

recordings.title: Chat: Qwen3-30B-A3B split across three DGX Sparks over RDMA
recordings.summary: The same scripted three-turn chat, with reasoning, split over all three Sparks (TASK-33): rank 0 on gx10-02 runs attention, the router and a third of the experts, and reaches gx10-03 and gx10-01 over RDMA on direct cables. It was recorded at 1.7 tokens/s because gx10-01's GPU was busy with another job; the same setup with that GPU free measured 27.5 tokens/s, so it plays at 16x by default. The per-rank call counts come from the frames and match the engine's own counters.

recordings.title: Soak: the first 3 minutes of the one-hour run (TASK-15)
recordings.summary: The first 6,000 steps of TASK-15's one-hour soak: OLMoE-1B-7B in two engine processes on gx10-02, linked over RDMA, repeating the golden prompts at 30.8 tokens/s. Every one of its 577 rounds gave the same tokens and logits. The full hour's recording (110,979 steps) is archived with the run.

recordings.title: Cross-machine: desktop GPU and a DGX Spark over the internet (TASK-15)
recordings.summary: TASK-15's 10-minute cross-machine run: rank 0 on a desktop's RTX 5070 Ti, rank 1 on gx10-02, linked over TCP through Tailscale's relay. It is slow (0.6 tokens/s, each layer waits about 100 ms on the relay), but its tokens matched transformers exactly. It plays at 10x speed by default.
